questions.q: What is a mixture?
questions.a: Two or more substances mixed in any ratio, each keeping its own properties, e.g. air, soil, salt water.

questions.q: How do mixtures differ from compounds?
questions.a: Mixtures have variable composition and no fixed boiling point; compounds have fixed composition and new properties.

questions.q: Name the two kinds of mixtures with examples.
questions.a: Homogeneous (uniform throughout, like salt solution) and heterogeneous (non-uniform, like sand and salt).

When is distillation used to separate a mixture?
questions.a: When the components differ in boiling points by about 25 deg C or more, e.g. acetone from water.

questions.q: What is fractional distillation for?
questions.a: Separating miscible liquids whose boiling points are close, like the fractions of petroleum or components of air.

questions.q: Give one everyday application of distillation.
questions.a: Obtaining pure drinking water by distillation, or separating alcohol from fermented mash in industry.

questions.q: What is chromatography used for?
questions.a: Separating coloured (or detectable) dissolved substances that travel at different speeds on an absorbent medium.

questions.q: On what principle does paper chromatography work?
questions.a: Different solutes are absorbed differently and move different distances with the solvent - separation by differential movement.

questions.q: Name two uses of chromatography.
questions.a: Separating dyes in ink, and detecting drugs or pigments in forensic and medical labs.

questions.q: When is a separating funnel used?
questions.a: To separate two immiscible liquids of different densities, like oil and water.

questions.q: On what property does the separating funnel rely?
questions.a: Difference in density - the denser liquid forms the lower layer and can be drained first.

questions.q: Give one example of a pair separated by a separating funnel.
questions.a: Kerosene (or mustard oil) and water; the water is drawn off from below.

questions.q: What is sublimation?
questions.a: A solid changing directly into vapour on heating, and vapour back to solid on cooling, without becoming liquid.

questions.q: Name two substances that sublime.
questions.a: Camphor and naphthalene (also iodine, ammonium chloride, dry ice).

questions.q: How does sublimation help separate mixtures?
questions.a: A sublimable component (like ammonium chloride) leaves the mixture as vapour and collects on a cold surface, away from salt or sand.

questions.q: What is centrifugation?
questions.a: Spinning a mixture fast so that denser particles settle at the bottom and lighter ones stay above.

questions.q: Name two uses of centrifugation.
questions.a: Separating cream from milk, and separating blood cells from plasma in labs.

questions.q: Why does the denser component settle first in a centrifuge?
questions.a: The rapid spin throws heavier particles outward more strongly than light ones, so they pack at the bottom.

questions.q: What is the Tyndall effect?
questions.a: Scattering of a beam of light by colloidal particles, making the beam's path visible.

questions.q: Why does a true solution not show the Tyndall effect?
questions.a: Its particles are too small (under 1 nm) to scatter light.

questions.q: Name two colloids that show the Tyndall effect.
questions.a: Milk and fog (also starch solution, smoke).
